sections.h2: Who handles property tax in Macoupin County?
sections.html:
Macoupin County splits the work between the Supervisor of Assessments, the Board of Review and the County Treasurer. The Supervisor of Assessments sits at 201 East Main in Carlinville, with a mailing address of P.O. Box 15, Carlinville, IL 62626, and answers at 217-854-8281. That office reviews what the township assessors do, equalizes values across the county and publishes assessment change notices.

Each year the Supervisor hands the assessment books to the Board of Review and prepares a tentative abstract for the Illinois Department of Revenue. The office also tracks every property transaction in the county, keeps parcel maps and exemption files, and holds the history of past owners. The Treasurer sends the bill and collects the money, so questions about what you owe go there and questions about what your house is worth go to the assessment side.

If you are selling, call both offices early. A title company will ask for the parcel number and the payoff of any unpaid installment before closing.

sections.h2: What does the Census say about Macoupin County homes?
sections.html:
Macoupin County is a rural, mostly owner-occupied county of about 43,748 people, according to the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate. QuickFacts counts 21,263 housing units, and 78.5 percent of occupied homes have an owner living in them. Homes that owners live in have a middle value of $138,200 for 2020-2024, while the middle household income is $70,805.

  • Households: 17,576, averaging 2.47 people each.
  • Median gross rent: $801 a month.
  • Median owner costs with a mortgage: $1,250 a month; without a mortgage: $566.
  • Mean commute: 27.5 minutes, which reflects how many residents drive to Springfield or the St. Louis area for work.
  • New construction is thin: the Census recorded 70 building permits in 2025.

Low turnover and few new builds mean the older housing stock sets the market, and assessors lean on recent sales of similar houses in the same township.

sections.h2: How is a Macoupin County house assessed?
sections.html:
A legal assessment outside Cook County is 33 1/3 percent of market value, with farmland and farm buildings treated separately. The county assessment page says all property is reassessed every four years and that changes in other years are still published. Township assessors do the first-line work, and the Supervisor reviews and equalizes what they produce.

To test your own number, divide the assessed value by the market value you would accept from a willing buyer. Compare that percentage with similar homes nearby. The county page lists four grounds that make a reasonable complaint:

  • The assessor's market value is higher than what the property would really sell for, which is easy to show if you bought recently or hold an appraisal.
  • Your assessment is a higher share of market value than the township or county median in a sales ratio study.
  • The record card has a wrong measurement, such as an incorrect lot or building size.
  • Similar neighboring properties carry lower assessments.

Mortgage holders must forward assessment change notices to borrowers within 15 days of receiving them, so a notice can reach you through the lender as well as the mail.

sections.h2: How do you appeal an assessment in Macoupin County?
sections.html:
Appeals start with a written complaint to the Macoupin County Board of Review, filed within 30 days of publication of the township assessment roll. A complaint sent by mail counts if the postmark is on or before the deadline. Use the Board's complaint form, sign it as the owner, and file a separate form for each parcel with your evidence attached.

After that the Board follows a set order, taken from its published rules:

  1. The Board docket numbers every properly filed complaint and may inspect the property.
  2. It mails a proposed notice with a tentative decision, or it schedules a hearing.
  3. If you disagree with the tentative decision, you have 10 days from the postmark on the proposed notice to ask for a hearing.
  4. The clerk of the Board schedules hearings and mails notice to you, then mails the final decision.

You may represent yourself or hire an attorney. Evidence the county suggests includes the transfer declaration, deed or purchase contract, an appraisal, a list of recent comparable sales with photographs and property record cards, and a copy of your own record card. If the Board's result still looks wrong, you can appeal in writing to the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board, or pay under protest and take the matter to court. The county notes that courts are more restrictive and rarely favor someone who skipped the administrative route.

One limit matters a lot: the Board of Review rules on the assessment, not on the tax bill. A complaint filed after the bill arrives is too late for that year.

sections.h2: What shapes the Macoupin County tax bill?
sections.html:
The bill comes from two inputs: your assessment and the amount your local taxing districts ask for. The county page stresses that the assessment is a way of dividing a fixed total among owners. When a school or township raises its levy, your bill moves even if your value did not.

Which district your house sits in is usually the biggest driver of the rate on your bill, so check the taxing bodies listed on it.

sections.h2: What is the county's background, and why does it matter to a seller?
sections.html:
Macoupin is named for Macoupin Creek and was carved out of Greene and Madison counties in 1829. It lies roughly midway between Springfield and St. Louis, and the Census Bureau placed it in the St. Louis metropolitan area in 2005 because of commuting. Farming, mainly corn and soybeans, remains the main industry. Coal mining once ran through many towns and has nearly disappeared.

Towns follow either a courthouse square layout, as in Carlinville, or a single main street. Some northern communities turned into bedroom towns for Springfield commuters, while the southern end looks toward the Metro East, so a sale in one corner of the county's 863 land square miles can draw a different buyer pool than a sale in another.

sections.h2: What should you do about unpaid tax before selling?
sections.html:
Ask the Macoupin County Treasurer for the installment dates and any balance, because the bill itself carries the due dates. Illinois counties sell unpaid taxes to tax buyers, so a delinquent balance is something a title company will want cleared before a deed is recorded. Ask the Treasurer or the County Clerk what is owed on your parcel.

If a bill never arrived, you still owe it, so contact the Treasurer for a duplicate. The practical order for a seller is simple: confirm what is paid, pull the parcel number from the bill, check that your homestead or senior exemption shows on it, and give all of that to the title company.

faqs.q: When must I file a Macoupin County assessment complaint?
faqs.a: The window closes 30 days after your township's roll is published, per the Board of Review rules. Mailed complaints count if postmarked on or before the last day. File one form per parcel and attach your evidence.

faqs.q: Can the Board of Review lower my tax bill?
faqs.a: No. It can only change the assessment, and the bill follows from that and from the rates set by your taxing districts. Once the bill is out, the assessment for that year is closed.

faqs.q: What is the assessment level in Macoupin County?
faqs.a: A legal assessment is 33 1/3 percent of market value, except for farmland and farm buildings. All property is reassessed every four years, and any change in a given year is published.

Call the Macoupin County Supervisor of Assessments at 217-854-8281, or write to P.O. Box 15, Carlinville, IL 62626. Start with your township assessor if you want to discuss the property record card first.

faqs.q: What is the median home value in Macoupin County?
faqs.a: $138,200 is the Census Bureau figure for 2020-2024. Over those same years the middle household income is $70,805, and owners live in 78.5 percent of the occupied homes.
